stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 7.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 303 K and 0.96 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 33.0 mL of 0.11 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.11 M NaOH.
9.2 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 117 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 6.9 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Fe electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Fe^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Fe^{2+} + 2e- -> Fe}$$ E° = -0.44 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Mg (Z = 12) and Al (Z = 13) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of $$\ce{Ba(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.001 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of $$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.001 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 15 g of $$\ce{Al2O3}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 102 g/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 22.7 g. The actual yield is 20.4 g. What is the percent yield?
A first-order reaction has a half-life of 31 min. Starting at 3.3 M, what is the concentration after 124 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: Why is solid NaCl a poor conductor while molten NaCl conducts?

options.text: Ions are fixed in the solid but mobile in the liquid

questions.stem: What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{SiH4}$$?

options.why: Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{H2O}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Why does I₂ have a higher boiling point than Br₂?

options.why: Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

options.text: I₂ has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so stronger London dispersion forces
options.why: Correct. Dispersion forces grow with polarizability.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.011 mol of solute in enough water to make 576 mL of solution?
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.
The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: A 30.1 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 40.4 mL of 0.168 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 5.4. In a solution at pH 4.9, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.8 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?

options.text: A larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 346 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.9 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 1.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.3 M, [B] = 0.8 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.67
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.667
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.667, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.667
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: Which process has a negative ΔS?
A reaction has K = 25. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 2 atoms of H in the formula.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CH4 16, O2 32, CO2 44, Ar 40.

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of manganese (Mn, Z = 25)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 25 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.58 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 207 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{KBr}$$ or $$\ce{MgF2}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because its ions have larger charges
They are equal because both are ionic

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; KBr has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.13 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.16 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2CO + O2 -> 2CO2}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.2) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 13.4 mL. What is the pH after 6.72 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Al/$$\ce{Al^{3+}}$$ and Pb/$$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.why: Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

options.text: Pb, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.

questions.explanation: Al (E° -1.66 V) is oxidized at the anode; Pb is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{AgBr}$$ is 5 \times 10^{-13}. What is its molar solubility in a solution that already contains 0.01 M of its anion?

options.why: That is the solubility in pure water.
The common ion's concentration dominates; no square root.
Correct. Ksp = s(c), so s = Ksp/c.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 3.2. A mixture has [A] = 0.2 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.5 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 3.57
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.79
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 1.79, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 1.79
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: 67 g of water at 54 °C is mixed with 177 g of water at 7 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.198 mol of solute in enough water to make 776 mL of solution?
On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 110 kJ/mol, the transition state at 258 kJ/mol and the products at 13 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 148, ΔH = -97, reverse Ea = 245 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 1.17 mol of gas in a 5 L container at 425 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 588, 1053, 1527, 10689 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 3 electrons, so it has 3 valence electrons.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: A compound (dinitrogen tetroxide) is 30.4% N, 69.6% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.
That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to NO2; the molecular formula is N2O4.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.46 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 6.35) and 0.42 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -14 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 5.65; K = 284. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, O2 32, Cl2 70.9, He 4.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of N in $$\ce{NH3}$$?

options.why: Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 5 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 3. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{3}$$, which has 15 electrons.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 4.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×4, so order 2 in B.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.4 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.2 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.387 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 242 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A solution has an absorbance of 0.324 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 81 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×2, so order 1 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3}$$, 98 g of $$\ce{Al}$$ reacts with 88 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{AlCl3}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -314 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -311 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Al/$$\ce{Al^{3+}}$$ and Ag/$$\ce{Ag+}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.text: Ag, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Al (E° -1.66 V) is oxidized at the anode; Ag is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 1 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = -100 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -96 J/(mol·K). Below what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).
Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.1 M and [I₂] = 0.7 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.02 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$, 86 g of $$\ce{H2}$$ reacts with 34 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{H2O}$$ can form?

options.why: Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.043 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 238 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 6.1 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 6070 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.807 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Fe²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Al.
Explain why the 1s peak of Al has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Mg.

rubric.criterion: Al has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Al has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Mg: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
